handoff.summary: Batch b03 adds three lane-adjacent records: mean (angular) motion as a 2π/T definition (Tatum's stated relation), circular-orbit specific-angular-momentum-squared derived from L = r·p_perp plus Eq. 13.7, and central mass from surface gravity (Eq. 13.2 rearranged, checked against the text's worked 5.95e24 kg and NASA polar values). assumptions: source assumption: uniform circular motion at constant angular speed, so one revolution (2π radians) takes exactly one period T (Tatum Fig. VIII.3 derivation context).
application profile: T is elapsed physical time in seconds on the same scale as the output; calendar day-counts must be converted to seconds before use, never inside this record.

constants.locator: Tatum §8.3: 'the relation between angular speed and period is ω = 2π/P'; double-precision expansion of 2π used in the expression.

gaps: Requires vocabulary extension: new meanings mean_motion and orbital_period (or reuse once defined), new unit rad/s (angle per time). No operator extension needed.

models.inverse_notes: Period solves as T = 6.283185307179586/n; substitution check with the ISS mean motion (n = 1.1321055e-3 rad/s) returns T = 5548.9 s against the published 5.55e3 s (0.02%, within oracle rounding). Requires n > 0 beyond the declared output domain. Do not publish the division as a separate record.
limitations: Uniform (mean) motion only; osculating angular speed on eccentric orbits varies within a revolution and needs the vis-viva treatment (deferred).
Output is an angular rate, not a frequency in cycles per unit time; the 2π distinguishes the two — do not drop it.

references.method: Independent route through trajectory geometry: n = v/r with the published ISS speed 7.67e3 m/s and radius 6.77e6 m (§13.4 example), giving 1.1329394e-3 rad/s. Tolerance 2e-6 (0.18%) covers 3-significant-figure print rounding.
references.provenance: Published speed and radius combined through the v = n·r identity — independent of the 2π/T definition under test.

references.method: Independent route: n = v/r with NASA's mean orbital velocity 29.78 km/s and semimajor axis 149.598M km (Earth Fact Sheet) against T = 365.256 d = 31558118.4 s. Tolerance 1e-10 (0.05%) covers near-circular deviation and rounding.

assumptions: source assumption: circular orbit so the perpendicular velocity component equals the full orbital speed (v_perp = v); the §13.5 passage gives L = r·m·v_perp generally, and circular motion has no radial component.

derived combination: per-unit-mass angular momentum h = r·v from the §13.5 passage, squared and combined with the §13.4 circular speed v² = G·M/r (Eq. 13.7) to give h² = G·M·r; both parent statements are source-backed, the two-line combination is the curator's derivation and is shown here.
Central mass M is a supplied input for a stated body and epoch.

models.inverse_notes: Radius solves as r = h2/(6.67e-11*M); substitution check with the (r·v)²-route ISS value (h2 = 2.6962991e21 m⁴/s², M = 5.96e24 kg) returns r = 6.784e6 m against 6.77e6 m (0.2%, within oracle rounding). Mass solves as M = h2/(6.67e-11*r). Requires h2 > 0 beyond the declared output domain. Do not publish rearrangements as separate records.
limitations: Circular orbits only; on eccentric orbits the (constant) angular momentum is r·v_perp at each point, not r·v, and this record must not be applied there.
Specific (per-unit-orbiter-mass) quantity; total angular momentum needs the orbiter mass factor and is not this record.
Ideal two-body motion only; torques, drag and perturbations excluded.

references.method: Independent route through the §13.5 angular-momentum passage: h = r·v with the published ISS radius 6.77e6 m and speed 7.67e3 m/s, squared to 2.6962991e21 m⁴/s². Tolerance 1e19 (0.37%) covers 3-significant-figure print rounding.

relationship.translation_notes: For circular motion v_perp = v, so h = r·v and h² = r²·v² = r²·(G·M/r) = G·M·r. The two parent equations are transcribed; the substitution is the curator's two-line derivation, labeled here rather than attributed to the source. Output name carries the square (h2). G inlined as the printed literal with constants metadata; no conversion inlined — coherent in base SI units. Dimensional check: (L³/(M·T²))·M·L = L⁴/T².

assumptions: source assumption: near-surface free fall where the separation of centers equals the body radius (r = R_E, Fig. 13.7) and the falling mass m cancels, so surface gravity depends only on the body (Eq. 13.2).

application profile: g is the measured free-fall acceleration at the surface and R the volumetric-mean-equivalent spherical radius; rotation/apparent-weight corrections are excluded (see limitations).

constants.locator: §13.2 Example 'Masses of Earth and Moon' prints G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

gaps: Requires vocabulary extension: new meanings surface_gravity and body_radius (or reuse once defined). Shares central_mass with the dynamical records: gravimetric (g·R²/G) and orbital (4π²a³/G·T²) mass determinations are complementary, not duplicates.

models.inverse_notes: Surface gravity solves as g = 6.67e-11*M/R**2 (Eq. 13.2 itself); substitution check with the text values (M = 5.96e24 kg, R = 6.37e6 m) returns g = 9.797 m/s² against 9.80 m/s². Radius solves as R = sqrt(M*6.67e-11/g) — sqrt halves dimensions correctly. Requires M > 0, g > 0 beyond the declared domains. Do not publish rearrangements as separate records.
limitations: Spherical, non-rotating idealization: the text notes g varies equator-to-pole (~0.5%) and apparent weight differs under rotation (§13.2); high-precision geodesy needs those corrections, not this record.
Scoped to the surface radius; the identical altitude form (text's 8.67 m/s² ISS-altitude example) is a different stated context and is not claimed here.
Requires an independently measured G (Cavendish tradition); before G, no absolute masses were knowable (source significance note).

references.method: Published worked result M_E = 5.95e24 kg from the §13.2 example (g = 9.80 m/s², R_E = 6.37e6 m). The 3-significant-figure inputs reproduce the text value; tolerance 2e22 (0.34%) covers print rounding.
references.provenance: Published worked result; checks the rearranged transcription against the source's own computation.

references.method: NASA polar surface acceleration 9.832 m/s² with polar radius 6356.752 km (Earth Fact Sheet) against the NASA tabulated mass 5.9722e24 kg. Tolerance 2e22 (0.33%) covers the spherical-form approximation on oblate-body values plus rounding.

G inlined as the printed literal with constants metadata; no conversion inlined — coherent in base SI units. Dimensional check: (L/T²)·L²/(L³/(M·T²)) = M. Output reuses the central_mass quantity shared with the orbital records by design (see integration).

sources.evidence: Substitutes mg into Newton's law to get g = GM_E/r² (Eq. 13.2), takes r = R_E at the surface, and works M_E = g·R_E²/G = 5.95e24 kg from g = 9.80 m/s² and R_E = 6.37e6 m; notes Earth also accelerates toward the object (neglected for m << M) and that G (Cavendish 1798) made absolute masses knowable.
